newsitem.title: USA: Clinton names Green Beret to head Joint Chiefs.
newsitem.headline: Clinton names Green Beret to head Joint Chiefs.

text.p: Ending a search made more difficult by the turmoil over sex in the military, President Bill Clinton on Thursday selected Army Gen. Henry Shelton to be chairman of the military Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Shelton, a tough Green Beret paratrooper who led U.S. forces in Haiti, would be the third army man in a row to fill a job that usually rotates among the army, navy and air force.

In announcing that he had decided to name the 55-year-old special forces commander to be the top U.S. military officer, Clinton said Shelton brought "unique perspective" to the job because of his expertise in unconventional warfare.

"Over more than three decades of service to our nation, he (Shelton) has distinguished himself as a decorated soldier, an innovative thinker, a superb commander. From Vietnam to Desert Storm, he has proven his skill and courage in combat," Clinton said at a White House Rose Garden ceremony.

Shelton's selection to succeed Army Gen. John Shalikashvili when his term as chairman expires at the end of September came five weeks after Air Force Gen. Joseph Ralston, vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs, withdrew from the running.
Ralston -- Defence Secretary William Cohen's first choice for the post -- asked that he not be considered after an adulterous affair in his background came to light.

The disclosure followed the forced resignation of Air Force Lt. Kelly Flinn, the first woman B-52 pilot, who otherwise would have faced court martial on charges arising from her love affair with a married man.
Clinton did not mention the sex scandals that have bedevilled the military since the Navy's Tailhook sexual harrassment case in the early 1990s.

After thanking the Polish-born Shalikashvili for his long service to the nation, Clinton said the new chairman-designate would guide the armed forces in a mission environment that includes peacekeeping duties, dealing with terrorism and curbing the spread of weapons of mass destruction.
If confirmed by the Senate, Shelton would jump from leading elite commando forces in the Tampa, Fla.-based U.S. Special Operations Command to being top man at the Pentagon.

"Over more than three decades of service to our nation, he (Shelton) has distinguished himself as a decorated soldier, an innovative thinker, a superb commander. From Vietnam to Desert Storm, he has proven his skill and courage in combat," Clinton said as Shelton and Shalikashvili stood beside him.
Cohen and other members of the Joint Chiefs also attended the brief announcement ceremony, which was held before the president left on a trip to Pennsylvania, Illinois and Arkansas.

Clinton said that Shelton's extensive experience in joint military operations and building coalitions with other nations "give him invaluable tools to serve as chairman in our more interdependent world."
"As the first commander of the U.S.-led multinational force in Haiti, his qualities personified the best of America -- strong and skilful, with great sensitivity, and no nonsense," he said.

Shelton, a native of Tarboro, North Carolina, who goes by the nickname "Hugh," is not a graduate of the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. Instead, he holds a degree in textile engineering from North Carolina State University and a master's degree from Auburn University in Alabama.
